messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 74
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Welder
- Trauma Type: Civilian in war zone
- Pcl5: 60

# The Weight of Remembering

Sanh sits in the office with his weathered hands folded in his lap, the calluses and burn scars from decades of welding work visible even in the soft afternoon light. At seventy-four, he has the posture of someone who has spent a lifetime bending over metal, though lately he finds himself hunched in a different way—as if carrying something invisible on his shoulders.

He came to the United States in 1975, though he rarely speaks about the year before that. When pressed gently about his history, he explains that he was a civilian in Saigon during the final months of the war. He was twenty-three then, working as a metalworker, helping repair gates and tools for his neighborhood. He had a fiancée, Linh, and they planned to marry that spring.

The city fell in April. Sanh's voice becomes very quiet when he describes the sounds—not the explosions, he says, but the silence after. The way people moved through the streets like ghosts. He and Linh managed to escape on one of the last boats, crammed with thousands of others, and they eventually made their way to California. They married in 1976 in a small ceremony. They have been together for nearly fifty years.

Sanh learned to weld because it was practical work, honest work. For decades, he threw himself into it completely—early mornings, late nights, building a reputation as someone meticulous and reliable. His hands knew what to do. The repetitive motion, the focus required, the way metal could be transformed into something solid and useful—all of it felt purposeful in a way that helped him move forward. Linh would say he was married to his work, and she said it with understanding rather than bitterness.

He retired five years ago, and that is when things began to change. Without the structure of the workshop, without the consuming focus of his craft, the silence returned. Not the literal silence of 1975, but something equally suffocating. He started waking at three in the morning, his heart racing, convinced he heard sirens or voices shouting in Vietnamese. Linh would find him standing at the kitchen window in the dark, watching the street.

The nightmares are vivid and specific. He dreams of searching for Linh in crowds of people he doesn't recognize, calling her name but hearing only his own voice echoing back. He dreams of fire—sometimes the welding torch, sometimes something else entirely. He wakes gasping, and it takes him several minutes to remember where he is, that he is safe, that Linh is sleeping beside him.

During the day, he is irritable in ways that confuse and sadden him. Linh will ask him a simple question about dinner, and he snaps at her. Loud noises—a car backfiring, a neighbor's construction—send electricity through his body. He finds himself avoiding the Vietnamese market they used to visit together, avoiding the community center where old friends gather. He tells himself it is just getting old, that everyone feels tired and withdrawn. But he knows it is more than that.

He has stopped welding entirely, even small projects in his garage. When he looks at his tools now, he feels something between longing and dread. His hands, which spent fifty years transforming metal into purpose, now feel empty. He spends his days watching television, though he rarely remembers what he has watched. Linh worries. She has suggested he come talk to someone, and after months of resistance, he has finally agreed.

Sanh is not sure why he is here, exactly. He survived. He built a life. He does not understand why the past keeps reaching into the present, pulling him backward into a place he has spent five decades trying to leave behind.
